comparison: Both strongly support the scRNA-seq findings showing ETBR expression in SGCs and ET-1 in vascular cells (C7, C8, C52, C53, C71-C77). OpenEval emphasizes validation through immunofluorescence and RNA in situ hybridization, while peer reviewers affirm the main conclusion is 'well supported' and note the importance of vascular signals. High agreement on cellular localization data.

Both support the ex vivo culture findings (C9, C54, C80, C85) showing ETBR inhibition promotes axon growth. OpenEval provides detailed quantitative assessment of both mixed and explant cultures. Peer reviewers accept these findings as 'convincing evidence' and note the study is 'well-executed,' though Reviewer 2 suggests improved presentation of representative images.

Strong agreement on in vivo regeneration data (C10, C56, C90, C91, C94). Both recognize Bosentan promotes regeneration while Ambrisentan does not, supporting ETBR specificity. OpenEval details the quantitative measurements and controls. Peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing' and affirm the main conclusion about ETBR as a 'default brake on axon regrowth.'

Both support the ETAR vs ETBR specificity findings (C92, C95, C104). OpenEval emphasizes the lack of effect with selective ETAR antagonism indicates ETBR is the relevant target. Peer Reviewer 3 notes 'comparison with an ETAR-specific antagonist suggests primary involvement of the ET-1/ETBR pathway.' Agreement on receptor specificity.

Both support findings on age-related regeneration deficits and rescue with ETBR inhibition (C11, C117, C118). OpenEval emphasizes restoration to adult levels in aged mice. Peer reviewers affirm the conclusion about ETBR 'contribut[ing] to the age-related decline in regenerative capacity' is 'well supported by the data.'

Perfect claim overlap (C100, C101, C152) regarding IENFD measurements. Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes only a trend without statistical significance and limited sample size. Peer reviewers do not explicitly validate or challenge this finding, and the manuscript uses speculative language ('may accelerate'). Agreement on uncertain status.

Both support DRC findings (C108, C109) showing ETBR inhibition improves regeneration in central injury models. OpenEval notes the response differs between injury types. Peer Reviewer 3 implicitly accepts DRC results when noting effects 'in mouse models of nerve injury' without limiting to peripheral injury only.

Both support snRNA-seq findings on age-related SGC changes (C12, C127). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive analysis with appropriate quality control and statistical testing. Peer Reviewer 3 notes 'snRNA sequencing and TEM analysis reveal a decline in SGC numbers...and transcriptional reprogramming' and describes the study as 'well-executed.'

Both support transcriptional profiling data showing age-related changes in SGCs (C58, C122-C126). OpenEval details GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses. Peer Reviewer 3 accepts the 'transcriptional reprogramming that may impair their pro-regenerative capacity.' No challenges to pathway analysis interpretation.

Both support TEM findings (C132-C135) showing decreased SGC width and nuclei number with age. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative analysis and adequate sample sizes. Peer Reviewer 3 notes 'TEM analysis reveal a decline in SGC numbers, morphological changes' as part of well-executed study. Agreement on structural evidence.

Both support Cx43 correlation data (C13, C14, C60, C143-C145) but note limitations. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but acknowledges correlation rather than causation. Peer reviewers accept the observational data but Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'no direct evidence' and 'no functional evidence' for causal mechanism. Agreement on correlative nature.

Both support findings (C96, C97) that ETBR levels don't change after injury. OpenEval emphasizes this indicates tonic inhibitory role. Reviewer 2 asks about this finding, seeking clarification on interpretation ('Does it mean that its endogenous function is to limit the spontaneous sensory axon regeneration?'), indicating acceptance of the data.

Both support in vitro findings (C102, C103) showing ETBR inhibition enhances axon growth from naive and conditioned neurons. OpenEval provides detailed assessment. Reviewer 2 accepts the data and requests discussion comparing in vitro and in vivo models, indicating acceptance with interest in contextual interpretation.

Both address age-related changes in ET-1 levels (C111). OpenEval supports elevated ET-1 in aged DRG. Reviewer 2 asks 'does the protein level of ETBR or its ligand change during aging?' indicating interest. The ET-1 increase data are presented and not challenged, supporting age-related ligand elevation.

Both address ETBR protein changes with age (C112) and rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes inconsistent results depending on normalization method. Reviewer 2's question about whether ETBR levels change with aging suggests this remains unresolved. Agreement on uncertain status of ETBR protein changes.

Both rate mechanistic link between ETBR and Cx43 (C149, C178) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes correlation is demonstrated but causal relationship not established, lacking Cx43 manipulation experiments. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'no direct evidence' and 'no functional evidence' for the mechanism. Reviewer 3 requests additional experiments. Strong agreement on incomplete mechanistic evidence.

Both rate ligand identity claims (C154-C156, C159) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes functional contribution of each ligand not tested and appropriately qualified as hypotheses. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'it cannot be excluded that ET-3 in fibroblasts is relevant' and notes 'both ET-1 and ET-3 participate' is discussed but not proven. Agreement on speculative nature.

Both address vascular permeability mechanism (C161) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval includes this among speculative hypotheses about additional mechanisms. Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'the possibility that the ET-1/ETBR pathway modulates vascular permeability...is discussed' but not directly tested. Agreement on speculative status.

Both strongly support the main conclusion (C162, C163) that ETBR acts as a brake on regeneration. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on convergent evidence from multiple systems. Editor states 'convincing evidence that it functions as a default brake,' Reviewer 3 affirms 'main conclusion...is well supported by the data.' Strong agreement on central finding.

Both support therapeutic potential claims (C63, C64, C186). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but notes appropriately qualified as speculative. Editor emphasizes 'since Bosentan is an FDA-approved drug, these findings could have therapeutic value,' and Reviewer 3 notes findings 'are likely to attract the interest of a broad readership.' Agreement on translational potential.

OpenEval evaluates claims about DRG vascularization (C65-C67) as SUPPORTED by citations and imaging data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as this anatomical context is accepted without specific comment by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates claims about SGC-neuron contact in culture systems (C78, C79, C84) as SUPPORTED, noting the explant model provides stronger evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific methodological claims.

OpenEval evaluates extensive additional background, context, and speculative mechanism claims (C99, C106-C107, C110, C129-C131, C137-C142, C164-C177, C179-C184) as SUPPORTED where factual and appropriately qualified where speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation systematically addresses these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates claim C75 about literature validation of scRNA-seq findings as SUPPORTED by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as this represents validation against existing literature rather than primary findings.

OpenEval evaluates claim C57 about Bosentan being a dual antagonist as SUPPORTED by citation and general knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as this factual claim about the drug is accepted without specific comment.

OpenEval evaluates claim C153 about SGC-mediated effects in explants as SUPPORTED with appropriate qualification. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this mechanistic interpretation of the explant model.
